# QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via Quality–Diversity

Takashi Ishida Affiliation: Sakana AI    Taro Makino Affiliation: Sakana
AI    Issa Sugiura Affiliation: Sakana AI

###### Abstract

Open-ended search combined with foundation models has produced advances
such as faster algorithms, new results on open mathematical problems,
and self-improving agents. We extend this paradigm to recommendation for
decision-making, focusing on decisions where the set of possible choices
is fixed but the reasons for choosing them are not. In high-stakes
decisions, e.g., which company to acquire or which customer to target,
comparing diverse, well-reasoned options can be more useful than a
single ranked list. We formalize _open-ended recommendation_ as building
a diverse, high-quality set of recommendations, each an item together
with a _hypothesis_, a natural-language reason why the item fits the
needs of a decision maker. We propose QD-Rec, a quality–diversity method
that selects items with a contextual bandit and generates hypotheses
with a foundation model from earlier ones kept in an archive as stepping
stones. A new recommendation enters the archive if it is novel or better
than its nearest neighbor. Across M&A, customer targeting, and paper and
book recommendation, QD-Rec gives the highest mean quality and builds
the largest archive in most settings.

![[Uncaptioned image]](2610.23470v2/assets/github.png)  Code:
[github.com/SakanaAI/QD-Rec](https://github.com/SakanaAI/QD-Rec)

## 1 Introduction

Open-ended search continually produces novel and increasingly capable or
diverse discoveries, and each can serve as a stepping stone for further
discovery ([Stanley and Lehman, 2015](#bib.bib42); [Hughes et al.,
2024](#bib.bib17)). Foundation models can act as the generator in this
search, drawing on earlier candidates to write new ones. This approach
has found candidates that no single query to the model would produce,
including creative text ([Bradley et al., 2024](#bib.bib5)), adversarial
prompts for red teaming ([Samvelyan et al., 2024](#bib.bib38)), tasks
that reveal a model’s capabilities ([Lu et al., 2025](#bib.bib29)), loss
functions ([Lu et al., 2024](#bib.bib28)), faster algorithms ([Novikov
et al., 2025](#bib.bib33)), new mathematical constructions
([Romera-Paredes et al., 2024](#bib.bib37); [Novikov et al.,
2025](#bib.bib33)), agent designs ([Hu et al., 2025](#bib.bib16)), and
self-improving agents ([Zhang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib48); [Wang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib45); [Zhang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib49)).

We ask whether open-ended search can extend to recommendation for
decision-making. Unlike open-ended generation, where the model generates
new candidates, many decisions are choices from a fixed pool of
candidates: an acquirer chooses among the companies that exist, a reader
among the papers already written, a marketer among the customers. At
first glance, this leaves no room for open-endedness, since the pool is
finite and known in advance. However, only the items are fixed. The same
item can be chosen for many different reasons, so the search over
reasons is still open-ended.

We therefore treat recommendation for such decisions as an open-ended
search over item–hypothesis pairs. A _hypothesis_ is a natural-language
explanation of why an item fits the decision maker’s profile, such as
the profile of one acquirer or one reader. The search returns a diverse,
high-quality set of such pairs for a single profile, rather than one
ranked list of items. We call this problem _open-ended recommendation_.
In high-stakes decisions, people need to compare candidate items
together with the reasons for choosing them ([Aggarwal,
2016](#bib.bib2)). We evaluate the set by its quality and diversity,
following the quality–diversity (QD) view of _illuminating_ a space of
alternatives ([Mouret and Clune, 2015](#bib.bib32)).

Open-ended recommendation has two properties that make open-ended search
a good fit. First, evaluation is costly: we learn a recommendation’s
value only by writing its hypothesis and judging it, so we cannot simply
score every possible recommendation in advance and sort them. The system
must therefore decide which item to evaluate next and learn from each
result. Second, the space is larger than the pool: each item allows
unlimited hypotheses, so even evaluating every item once would leave
most of the space unexplored. Good hypotheses often come from adapting
or combining earlier ones, so keeping modest intermediate hypotheses as
stepping stones can help ([Lehman and Stanley, 2011](#bib.bib23);
[Stanley and Lehman, 2015](#bib.bib42)). QD and novelty search are well
suited to such problems ([Risi et al., 2025](#bib.bib36)). [Gallotta et
al. (2024)](#bib.bib13) explored QD for generating and recommending
spaceship designs through grammar-based evolution guided by user
preferences. We extend this connection between QD and recommendation to
decisions involving a fixed pool of existing items, using foundation
models to generate and refine hypotheses for recommending them.¹¹ 1
Evolutionary methods have been applied to decision-making more broadly,
for example to evolve neural networks that prescribe interventions
against COVID-19 ([Risi et al., 2025](#bib.bib36), Section 6.4).

Figure 1: Overview of QD-Rec. Each iteration selects an item from the
fixed pool $`\mathcal{C}`$ via a diversity-aware bandit, generates a
hypothesis with an LLM conditioned on archive exemplars, which act as
parents (an evolutionary operator), and judges the new pair against its
$`k`$ nearest neighbors: a novel pair is added immediately; a non-novel
one survives only by winning a pairwise duel against its neighbor.

We introduce QD-Rec, a quality–diversity search method for open-ended
recommendation (Figure
[1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via Quality–Diversity")).
In QD-Rec, an LLM called the _proposer_ writes hypotheses, and an LLM
judge or humans score them. Each iteration has three steps. A contextual
bandit selects an item from the candidate pool, balancing items that
look promising against regions the archive has not yet covered. The
proposer generates a hypothesis for that item, building on a few earlier
hypotheses from the archive. The new recommendation is kept if it is
novel, or if it is better than its nearest neighbor in the archive.
Novelty and quality are thus judged _locally_, by comparison with nearby
recommendations.

Our contributions are: (i) we formalize _open-ended recommendation_ as a
quality–diversity search over item–hypothesis pairs, where the items
come from a fixed pool; (ii) we propose QD-Rec, with two ablations
isolating its components (Table
[1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Methods. ‣ 5.1 Setup ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via Quality–Diversity"));
and (iii) across four domains and two proposers, QD-Rec gives the
highest mean quality in most LLM-judged settings, usually builds the
largest archive, and outperforms diversity-aware rerankers on
human-rated quality.

## 2 Background and Related Work

We briefly review quality–diversity methods and novelty search,
evolutionary loops built around foundation models, and recommender
systems.

##### Quality–diversity and novelty search.

Quality–diversity (QD) methods aim to discover a _set_ of
high-performing yet diverse solutions rather than a single optimum.
Multi-dimensional Archive of Phenotypic (MAP) Elites “illuminates” a
search space by maintaining an archive and retaining elites across
behavioral niches ([Mouret and Clune, 2015](#bib.bib32)). Novelty search
emphasizes exploration by rewarding behavioral novelty, providing a
mechanism for stepping-stone trajectories in which intermediate
solutions enable later progress ([Lehman and Stanley,
2011](#bib.bib23)). Recent work continues to revisit local competition
and novelty definitions in QD, including dominated novelty variants
([Bahlous-Boldi et al., 2025](#bib.bib4)), and to reduce dependence on
hand-designed behavioral descriptors through methods such as AURORA
([Grillotti and Cully, 2022](#bib.bib14)) and dimensionless MAP-Elites
([Dharna et al., 2025](#bib.bib10)).

##### Foundation models in evolutionary loops.

A growing family of systems places a frozen large model inside an
evolutionary or QD loop as a proposal operator or mutator, keeping an
archive of artifacts that the model conditions on to propose the next:
diverse creative text in QDAIF ([Bradley et al., 2024](#bib.bib5)),
adversarial prompts in Rainbow Teaming ([Samvelyan et al.,
2024](#bib.bib38)), code and program search in ELM ([Lehman et al.,
2023](#bib.bib24)) and FunSearch ([Romera-Paredes et al.,
2024](#bib.bib37)), algorithm discovery in AlphaEvolve ([Novikov et al.,
2025](#bib.bib33)), sample-efficient program evolution in ShinkaEvolve
([Lange et al., 2026](#bib.bib21)), open-ended evaluation tasks in
Automated Capability Discovery ([Lu et al., 2025](#bib.bib29)), and
agent designs in ADAS ([Hu et al., 2025](#bib.bib16)).²² 2 In
evolutionary loops, foundation models can also play roles other than
proposing new artifacts. In CycleQD ([Kuroki et al., 2025](#bib.bib20))
and AC/DC ([Dai et al., 2026](#bib.bib9)), they are themselves the
artifacts being evolved. In a replication of Picbreeder ([Earle et al.,
2026](#bib.bib11)), vision–language models take the place of its human
evaluators. A separate line of work is _self-referential_: STOP
([Zelikman et al., 2024](#bib.bib47)), the Darwin Gödel Machine ([Zhang
et al., 2026a](#bib.bib48)), the Huxley–Gödel Machine ([Wang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib45)), and Hyperagents ([Zhang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib49))
turn the search on the machinery itself, so the improved scaffold or
agent performs the next round of improvement. QD-Rec belongs to the
first group, with item–hypothesis pairs as the artifacts. However, these
systems create new artifacts, while QD-Rec must choose its items from a
fixed pool.

##### Recommender systems.

Recommenders learn either _offline_, from a fixed dataset of past
interactions ([Aggarwal, 2016](#bib.bib2)), or _online_, as a sequential
decision problem with an exploration–exploitation trade-off, usually
modeled as a (contextual) bandit ([Lattimore and Szepesvári,
2020](#bib.bib22); [Agarwal et al., 2009](#bib.bib1); [Li et al.,
2010](#bib.bib25); [Agrawal and Goyal, 2013](#bib.bib3); [Song et al.,
2022](#bib.bib41)). Previous work has also combined bandits with QD to
select parents or bins from an archive ([Sfikas et al.,
2021](#bib.bib39); [Gallotta et al., 2024](#bib.bib13)) and to choose
how to generate new solutions ([Cully, 2021](#bib.bib8); [Gaier et al.,
2020](#bib.bib12)). Whereas these methods generate the candidate
solutions themselves, QD-Rec uses a contextual bandit to select existing
items rather than parents or generation strategies. QD-Rec then
generates hypotheses for the selected items. As in QD, it is evaluated
by its final archive.

Orthogonally, a long line of work treats diversity, novelty, coverage,
and serendipity as first-class objectives ([McNee et al.,
2006](#bib.bib30); [Ziegler et al., 2005](#bib.bib53); [Vargas and
Castells, 2011](#bib.bib43); [Kaminskas and Bridge, 2016](#bib.bib19)),
pursued offline by re-ranking ([Carbonell and Goldstein,
1998](#bib.bib6); [Chen et al., 2018](#bib.bib7)) and online by
diversity-aware bandits ([Radlinski et al., 2008](#bib.bib35); [Liu et
al., 2020](#bib.bib27)). These methods diversify the list shown to a
user; QD-Rec instead enforces diversity at archive admission, following
recent QD systems ([Lu et al., 2025](#bib.bib29); [Dharna et al.,
2025](#bib.bib10)): an LLM judges whether each new pair is novel
relative to its nearest archive neighbors. Finally, explainable
recommendation adds a natural-language explanation to each recommended
item ([Zhang and Chen, 2020](#bib.bib51)), and so do LLM recommenders
that reason before choosing or justify afterward. QD-Rec also pairs each
item with a reason, but it does so inside an evolutionary loop.

## 3 Open-Ended Recommendation

Let $`\mathcal{C}=\{c_{1},\dots,c_{N}\}`$ be a fixed candidate pool
(e.g., companies for M&A, customer profiles for targeting, papers, or
books), and let $`\pi`$ be the _profile_ of one decision maker. A
_hypothesis_ $`h\in\mathcal{H}`$ is a natural-language explanation of
why an item fits $`\pi`$, and the hypothesis space $`\mathcal{H}`$ is
unbounded. A _recommendation_ is a pair
$`(c,h)\in\mathcal{C}\times\mathcal{H}`$, so the same item can be
recommended several times with different hypotheses. Its quality
$`q(c,h)`$ is a score from a human or an LLM judge, for example on a 0
to 10 scale. The score is known only after the hypothesis is written and
evaluated, and each evaluation is costly. Given $`\pi`$ and
$`\mathcal{C}`$, the task is to return a set
$`\mathcal{S}\subset\mathcal{C}\times\mathcal{H}`$ of recommendations
that have high quality and differ from one another, using at most $`T`$
evaluations. Section
[5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1 Setup ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via Quality–Diversity")
defines the metrics for quality and diversity.

## 4 QD-Rec

We present QD-Rec, an _archive-based quality–diversity (QD) method_ for
open-ended recommendation. QD-Rec keeps an archive $`\mathcal{A}`$ of
retained recommendations and returns it as $`\mathcal{S}`$ at the end of
the run. Each new entry is compared only with its nearest neighbors in
the archive to decide whether it is kept. Each archive entry $`x`$
stores a recommendation $`(c,h)`$, its embedding
$`e=\mathrm{Embed}(c,h)`$, and its quality score $`q(x)`$. The embedding
is computed from a structured item profile followed by the hypothesis
text. We use cosine similarity
$`\mathrm{sim}(x_{i},x_{j})=\langle e_{i},e_{j}\rangle/(\|e_{i}\|\,\|e_{j}\|)`$
to define these neighborhoods.

### 4.1 Local novelty, ranking, and archive update

At each step we propose a new pair by selecting an item $`c`$ and
generating a hypothesis $`h`$ (Section
[4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Item selection and hypothesis generation ‣ 4 QD-Rec ‣ QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via Quality–Diversity"));
we write $`x_{\text{new}}=(c,h,e_{\text{new}})`$ with
$`e_{\text{new}}=\mathrm{Embed}(c,h)`$ for the proposed entry (its
quality estimate is not yet known at this point). We retrieve the $`k`$
nearest neighbors from the archive,

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\mathcal{N}_{k}(x_{\text{new}})=\operatorname*{arg\,max}^{k}_{x\in\mathcal{A}}\,\mathrm{sim}(x_{\text{new}},x).
``` |  |

The archive update then proceeds in the following two steps:

- •
  *Novelty check*: an LLM judge is prompted with the profile $`\pi`$,
  the new entry, and its $`k`$ nearest neighbors, and returns a binary
  decision $`\texttt{is\_novel}\in\{0,1\}`$ (with brief reasoning). A
  novel entry is admitted immediately; no comparison is made.
- •
  *Local quality comparison* (only when not novel): we use a blind
  pairwise duel: of the $`k`$ neighbors only the single *nearest* one is
  contested. It and $`x_{\text{new}}`$ are shuffled into two anonymous
  positions, pointwise scores are withheld, and the judge, never told
  which of the two is the newcomer, chooses the stronger under $`\pi`$
  (ties are not allowed). If $`x_{\text{new}}`$ wins it replaces that
  neighbor; otherwise it is discarded. Algorithm
  [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Simpler variants. ‣ 4.2 Item selection and hypothesis generation ‣ 4 QD-Rec ‣ QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via Quality–Diversity")
  writes this comparison as $`\mathrm{Better}_{\pi}`$. Separating the
  two questions keeps the retention comparison *blind* (the judge cannot
  favor or disfavor an entry for being new) and skips the comparison
  call entirely whenever the entry is novel.

This embedding-neighborhood admission scheme is inspired by recent
novelty-search/QD systems that use learned representations for
similarity and archive admission ([Lu et al., 2025](#bib.bib29); [Dharna
et al., 2025](#bib.bib10)).

The quality score $`q(x)`$ of each evaluated pair (Section
[3](#S3 "3 Open-Ended Recommendation ‣ QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via Quality–Diversity"))
has two uses. The bandit reward $`r(x)`$ is the score divided by the
maximum of its scale, so that rewards lie in $`[0,1]`$. Reported Quality
averages the score over the final archive, on its original scale.

### 4.2 Item selection and hypothesis generation

The archive mechanics above leave two decisions open: which item
$`c\in\mathcal{C}`$ to evaluate next, and how to generate a hypothesis
$`h`$ for it.

##### Item selection.

Each candidate item $`c`$ has a *precomputed candidate embedding*
$`\psi(c)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}`$, distinct from the archive-entry embedding
$`e`$ and taken to be L2-normalized. It embeds the item’s text: the
title and abstract of a paper, the title and description of a book, the
business description of a company, or the profile of a customer. We
model a scalar reward $`r\in[0,1]`$ by Bayesian linear regression,
$`r=\psi(c)^{\top}\theta+\epsilon`$ with
$`\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2})`$ and prior
$`\theta\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\lambda^{-1}I)`$. For the set $`\mathcal{D}`$
of evaluated pairs we maintain the sufficient statistics

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
A\;=\;\lambda I+\sigma^{-2}\!\!\sum_{(\psi,r)\in\mathcal{D}}\!\!\psi\psi^{\top},\qquad b\;=\;\sigma^{-2}\!\!\sum_{(\psi,r)\in\mathcal{D}}\!\!r\,\psi,\qquad\theta\mid\mathcal{D}\;\sim\;\mathcal{N}(A^{-1}b,\;A^{-1}),
``` |  |

and a new observation $`(\psi(c),r)`$ updates them in closed form:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
A\;\leftarrow\;A+\sigma^{-2}\,\psi(c)\psi(c)^{\top},\qquad b\;\leftarrow\;b+\sigma^{-2}\,r\,\psi(c).
``` |  |

Linear Thompson sampling ([Agrawal and Goyal, 2013](#bib.bib3)) then
draws $`\tilde{\theta}\sim\mathcal{N}(A^{-1}b,A^{-1})`$ at each step,
and, with a small modification for diversity, we select the candidate
that maximizes the *diversity-aware selection score*

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
s(c)\;=\;\psi(c)^{\top}\tilde{\theta}\;+\;\beta\,d(c,\mathcal{R}),\qquad d(c,\mathcal{R})\;=\;1-\max_{c^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}}\psi(c)^{\top}\psi(c^{\prime}),
``` |  | (1) |

where $`\mathcal{R}`$ collects the candidate embeddings of the current
archive. The bonus $`d(c,\mathcal{R})`$ is the cosine distance to the
*nearest* covered item (the standard nearest-neighbor novelty measure),
so it is large exactly when nothing similar has been archived yet, and
$`\beta\geq 0`$ trades this coverage of under-explored regions against
the sampled quality estimate $`\psi(c)^{\top}\tilde{\theta}`$. The
bandit *reward* is unchanged: after evaluation we update the posterior
using the normalized reward $`r(x)`$ defined above, so $`\beta`$ affects
only *which* items are chosen for evaluation, steering the archive to
spread rather than cluster. Setting $`\beta=0`$ recovers the plain
quality-only bandit; we use $`\beta=1`$ throughout. We warm-start the
posterior from the seed archive: each seed entry contributes one
observation $`(\psi(c),r(x))`$, using the same normalization.

An item can be selected more than once, because a new hypothesis for it
can receive a different quality score. The same item can also appear in
the archive several times.³³ 3 For an item already in the archive, the
bonus $`d(c,\mathcal{R})`$ is zero, so QD-Rec rarely selects it again.
In our runs, no final QD-Rec archive contains the same item twice. If a
new hypothesis for an item differs enough from the entries near it, the
novelty check admits it as a new entry.

##### Hypothesis generation (evolutionary operator).

Given the selected item $`c`$, we prompt the proposer LLM with the
profile $`\pi`$, the item $`c`$, and $`m`$ exemplars sampled uniformly
from the current archive. The prompt presents the exemplars as existing
hypotheses and instructs the model to apply one of three operators,
*mutate* (adapt one exemplar’s angle to $`c`$), *crossover* (combine
angles from several exemplars), or *explore* (propose an angle the
exemplars miss), so the archive acts as an evolving population ([Guo et
al., 2024](#bib.bib15); [Lehman et al., 2023](#bib.bib24)).

##### Simpler variants.

We also define two simpler variants of QD-Rec, which serve as ablations
of the full method. *Novelty+Evo* replaces the bandit with
uniform-random item selection. *Novelty* removes both the bandit and the
exemplars, so the proposer generates hypotheses zero-shot. All three
methods share the archive update of Section
[4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Local novelty, ranking, and archive update ‣ 4 QD-Rec ‣ QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via Quality–Diversity"),
and Table
[1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Methods. ‣ 5.1 Setup ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via Quality–Diversity")
compares them. Algorithm
[1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Simpler variants. ‣ 4.2 Item selection and hypothesis generation ‣ 4 QD-Rec ‣ QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via Quality–Diversity")
gives QD-Rec in full.

$`\mathcal{A}`$, iterations $`T`$, neighborhood size $`k`$, exemplars
$`m`$, diversity weight $`\beta\geq 0`$, prior precision $`\lambda`$,
noise variance $`\sigma^{2}`$; warm-start $`A=\lambda I`$, $`b=0`$ with
one observation $`(\psi(c),r(x))`$ per seed entry

1:  for $`t=1`$ to $`T`$ do

2:    Sample $`\tilde{\theta}\sim\mathcal{N}(A^{-1}b,\,A^{-1})`$ //
diversity-aware bandit item selection

3:
   $`c\leftarrow\arg\max_{c\in\mathcal{C}}\big[\psi(c)^{\top}\tilde{\theta}+\beta\,d(c,\mathcal{R})\big]`$

4:
   $`h\leftarrow\text{LLM}_{\text{mut}}(\pi,c,\text{SampleParents}(\mathcal{A},m))`$
// few-shot hypothesis generation

5:    $`x_{\text{new}}\leftarrow(c,h,\mathrm{Embed}(c,h))`$ // local
novelty + ranking archive update

6:    Obtain $`q(x_{\text{new}})`$; set
$`r\leftarrow r(x_{\text{new}})`$ // score scaled to $`[0,1]`$

7:
   $`\mathcal{N}_{k}\leftarrow k\text{NN}(x_{\text{new}},\mathcal{A})`$

8:
   $`\texttt{novel}\leftarrow\text{LLM}_{\text{novelty}}(\pi,x_{\text{new}},\mathcal{N}_{k})`$
// novelty first

9:    if novel then

10:     Add $`x_{\text{new}}`$ to $`\mathcal{A}`$ // admitted; no

11:    else if
$`\mathrm{Better}_{\pi}(x_{\text{new}},\ \text{nearest neighbor})`$ then

13:    end if

14:    $`A\leftarrow A+\sigma^{-2}\psi(c)\psi(c)^{\top}`$,

Algorithm 1 QD-Rec. The Novelty+Evo ablation uses uniform-random
selection from $`\mathcal{C}`$; Novelty additionally uses no exemplars
($`m=0`$).

### 4.3 Implementation details

To speed up experiments, we run the loop in parallel batches where
workers propose and evaluate candidates against a snapshot of the
current archive. To select a batch of $`B`$ items, we extend the
single-draw rule of Section
[4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Item selection and hypothesis generation ‣ 4 QD-Rec ‣ QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via Quality–Diversity"):
we take $`B`$ independent posterior draws
$`\tilde{\theta}_{1},\dots,\tilde{\theta}_{B}`$, and for each
$`\tilde{\theta}_{i}`$ select the candidate maximizing $`s(c)`$ while
excluding items already chosen in the batch and adding them to
$`\mathcal{R}`$, so the diversity bonus discourages near-duplicates
within a batch as well as against the archive. After each batch, we
reconcile results by filtering near-duplicate additions (above a
cosine-similarity threshold) and resolving replacement collisions
(multiple workers targeting the same neighbor). The bandit uses prior
precision $`\lambda=1`$ and noise standard deviation $`\sigma=0.1`$, the
novelty check uses $`k=3`$ nearest neighbors, and each run starts from
$`10`$ seed entries.

## 5 Experiments

We evaluate the three variants (Novelty, Novelty+Evo, QD-Rec; Table
[1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Methods. ‣ 5.1 Setup ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via Quality–Diversity"))
across four domains.

### 5.1 Setup

##### Common protocol.

Our main experiment uses claude-sonnet-5 as the hypothesis proposer; we
additionally report a weaker-proposer ablation that swaps in
claude-haiku-4-5. The judge is gpt-5.6-terra in *every* configuration
and domain, a different model family from both proposers, to prevent
self-preference bias ([Wataoka et al., 2024](#bib.bib46)). Proposer and
judge both run with reasoning effort set to high. The weak-proposer
ablation model does not support the effort parameter and runs without it
or extended thinking. We leave the temperature setting to the provider
default for claude-haiku-4-5. Each configuration runs $`1{,}000`$
evaluations (proposal–judge cycles) per method in all four domains,
executed in generations of up to $`20`$ parallel evaluations, with the
archive reconciled between generations (Section
[4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Implementation details ‣ 4 QD-Rec ‣ QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via Quality–Diversity")).
Novelty+Evo and QD-Rec condition each proposal on $`m=3`$ archive
exemplars. Runs are repeated for five random seeds. Each run begins from
a seed archive under the same profile $`\pi`$; the seed controls the
pipeline’s own sampling randomness (parent selection, item ordering)
while LLM sampling stays at the provider default, so across-seed spread
measures the stochasticity of the full pipeline.

We embed archive entries and candidate items with OpenAI’s
text-embedding-3-small at $`512`$ output dimensions, L2-normalized, and
use cosine similarity for $`k`$-nearest-neighbor retrieval.

##### Methods.

We evaluate the proposed method QD-Rec and its two ablations (Novelty,
Novelty+Evo) under matched evaluation budgets and shared hyperparameters
within each domain. Table
[1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Methods. ‣ 5.1 Setup ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via Quality–Diversity")
summarizes the three variants as an “ingredients” view: all share the
archive mechanics; Novelty+Evo adds the evolutionary few-shot operator,
and QD-Rec additionally adds diversity-aware bandit item selection.

Table 1: QD-Rec and its two ablations. All three use the same archive
update (Section
[4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Local novelty, ranking, and archive update ‣ 4 QD-Rec ‣ QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via Quality–Diversity")).

##### Domains.

We instantiate the framework on four fixed-pool domains, each realizing
the hypothesis $`h`$ in its native genre. The first, Goodreads, is a
*grounding check* whose quality signal is a real human rating rather
than an LLM judge; the other three are heterogeneous applied settings.
Full dataset construction (sources, filtering, pool sizes, and the
specific profiles used) is in Appendix
[C](#A3 "Appendix C Dataset details ‣ QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via Quality–Diversity").

- •
  Goodreads. The pool $`\mathcal{C}`$ is the children’s books a reader
  has rated ([Wan and McAuley, 2018](#bib.bib44)); the profile $`\pi`$
  is that reader (summarized from past reviews); $`h`$ is a reading memo
  on whether they would enjoy a book. Uniquely, quality is *not* an LLM
  judge but the reader’s own $`1`$–$`5`$ rating, held out of all prompts
  and used only as the reward and replacement signal (Appendix
  [C](#A3 "Appendix C Dataset details ‣ QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via Quality–Diversity")),
  testing whether QD still yields meaningful quality–diversity tradeoffs
  under a real human signal. This Quality measure evaluates the book for
  the reader, not the generated memo: changing the memo cannot change
  the rating, although it can affect novelty and archive geometry.
- •
  M&A target discovery. $`\mathcal{C}`$ is a universe of 6,332 US
  companies built from LSEG Workspace data (business descriptions,
  industry taxonomy, financials). The business descriptions average
  approximately 123 words. The profile $`\pi`$ is an acquirer (Walt
  Disney or JPMorgan Chase), and $`h`$ is an acquisition thesis (e.g.
  capability acquisition vs. market access vs. vertical integration).
  Deal sourcing motivates it: teams want a *diverse set of strategic
  theses* rather than a single shortlist.
- •
  Marketing. $`\mathcal{C}`$ is 10,000 synthetic customer profiles from
  California, sampled from NVIDIA Nemotron-Personas-USA ([Meyer and
  Corneil, 2025](#bib.bib31)). The customer profiles average
  approximately 685 words. The profile $`\pi`$ is a product (a desktop
  3D printer or an online upskilling subscription), and $`h`$ is a
  targeting hypothesis explaining why a profile is an attractive target
  for $`\pi`$, yielding a map of distinct targeting angles rather than a
  ranked list.
- •
  Paper-abstract exploration. $`\mathcal{C}`$ is the titles and
  abstracts of 17,511 papers accepted at ICLR 2026, ICML 2026 and
  NeurIPS 2025 ([Paper Copilot (2026), Jing Yang](#bib.bib34)), $`\pi`$
  a researcher profile (an open-endedness researcher or an applied
  researcher at an AI startup), and $`h`$ a research memo linking a
  paper to $`\pi`$. The scale of the AI literature motivates it:
  researchers need *diverse*, well-justified reading directions under
  limited time. Candidate embeddings for bandit item selection are
  precomputed from title+abstract; archive embeddings are computed from
  title+abstract+memo.

##### Evaluation.

Four metrics summarize a run’s final active archive.

- •
  Quality is the mean pointwise score of its entries: the judge score
  (0–10), or in Goodreads the reader’s real star rating (1–5).
- •
  Diversity is one minus the mean pairwise cosine similarity between
  archive-entry embeddings, computed in the original embedding space
  (the complement of the mean pairwise similarity used to quantify
  homogenization by [Jiang et al., 2025](#bib.bib18)).
- •
  Coverage is the fraction of occupied cells on a $`25{\times}25`$ grid
  over a 2D PCA projection (the maps of Figure
  [2(a)](#S5.F2.sf1 "Figure 2(a) ‣ Figure 2 ‣ Cost. ‣ 5.2 Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via Quality–Diversity")).
  For each profile, proposer, and trial seed, we fit PCA by full SVD on
  the union of all three variants’ active archives and use shared axis
  bounds padded by 1% on each side. Coverage is comparable across
  methods within that grid; separate profiles, proposers, and seeds use
  separate grids.
- •
  Archive size $`n`$ is the number of entries that survived admission.

##### Online evaluation protocol.

We score each recommendation during the search. QD-Rec uses these scores
to update its bandit and select subsequent candidates. Final Quality is
the mean of the scores already assigned to the recommendations retained
in the archive.

##### Main results.

QD-Rec gives the best mean Quality in most LLM-judged settings (Table
[2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5.2 Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via Quality–Diversity")),
often significantly better than both ablations, and it is never
significantly worse than the best variant. The gains are largest on M&A.
QD-Rec also builds the largest archive in most settings and often has
the best MAP-Elites coverage, so its higher Quality does not come from a
smaller, more selective archive. Its semantic Diversity is the best or
tied for best in every domain except M&A, where it is slightly lower. On
Goodreads, where Quality is the reader’s own star rating, the three
variants reach similar mean ratings. There, QD-Rec keeps this rating
while matching or beating both ablations on archive size, Diversity and
coverage.

##### Cost.

We measure cost as the API spend of a run in US dollars at list prices.
It covers every model call: the proposer, the quality judge, the novelty
check, the duel, and the embeddings. The three variants make the same
calls for each of the $`1{,}000`$ evaluations. They differ only in the
proposer prompt, which includes three archive exemplars in Novelty+Evo
and QD-Rec, and in how often a duel is needed. The bandit runs locally
and adds no API cost. The runs did not log token usage, so we estimate
the cost of each call type by re-sending a sample of $`840`$ archived
calls with the same models and settings. We then multiply by the exact
number of calls in each run. QD-Rec costs the same as Novelty+Evo, and
both cost about $`1.3\times`$ as much as Novelty. More than $`90\%`$ of
the difference comes from the proposer, because the exemplars roughly
triple its input. A single run costs between about \$13 (Novelty on
Goodreads with the claude-haiku-4-5 proposer) and \$62 (QD-Rec on
Marketing with the claude-sonnet-5 proposer). Goodreads is the cheapest
domain because its ratings replace the LLM judge and the duel.

##### Comparison to a no-learning baseline.

To ask whether the online learning and archive machinery earns its cost,
we compare against two training-free re-rankers, relevance-MMR
([Carbonell and Goldstein, 1998](#bib.bib6)) and a quality-weighted DPP
with greedy MAP inference ([Chen et al., 2018](#bib.bib7)), on
Goodreads, where Quality is a real human star rating. Sweeping each
baseline’s relevance–diversity weight $`\gamma`$,no setting of either
reaches any QD variant on Quality, and they approach QD-Rec’s semantic
Diversity only at their most diversity-favoring settings. The baselines
see no ratings while the QD variants query up to $`1{,}000`$, so the gap
reflects rating feedback and the archive together, not item selection
alone. Full setup and the per-setting table are in Appendix
[B](#A2 "Appendix B No-learning baselines: relevance-MMR and a quality-weighted DPP ‣ QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via Quality–Diversity").

##### Embedding-model sensitivity.

The embedding model defines the novelty neighborhoods, the Diversity
metric, the MAP-Elites grid and the bandit’s item features. We therefore
re-run one profile per domain with a different embedding model,
Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B truncated to the same $`512`$ dimensions
(claude-haiku-4-5 proposer, seed $`0`$, one run with batches of $`16`$
instead of $`20`$, due to the compute limits of the local machine that
runs the embedding model; Table
[3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Quality and archive size over the run. ‣ 5.2 Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via Quality–Diversity")).
The best variant on Quality and on archive size is the same as with the
original embeddings on all four profiles. Diversity is higher for every
variant, because the Qwen embeddings are spread more evenly. Diversity
and Coverage can therefore be compared only within one embedding space,
while the Quality and archive-size orderings are unchanged.

## 6 Conclusion

We introduced QD-Rec, an archive-based quality–diversity method for
open-ended recommendation, where the items are chosen with contextual
bandits, and the reasons for recommending them are searched
open-endedly. Across four domains, QD-Rec gave the best mean Quality in
most settings and usually built the largest archive. As a first work
along this line, we kept it relatively simple, and several directions
follow.

First, our bandit uses Bayesian linear regression to model reward from
fixed item embeddings. Neural contextual bandits ([Zhou et al.,
2020](#bib.bib52); [Zhang et al., 2021](#bib.bib50)) could capture
nonlinear relationships between these embeddings and reward. More
radically, the bandit could be discarded altogether in favor of a coding
agent that reads the archive directly, reasons over which regions look
exhausted and which look promising, and writes its own selection rule,
replacing a fixed parametric reward model with a policy that can be
inspected and revised in natural language. Second, exemplars are sampled
uniformly from the archive, and could instead be selected by quality,
recency, or how often they have already served as exemplars ([Earle et
al., 2026](#bib.bib11); [Zhang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib48)). Bandits
could also be used for parent selection, in addition to item selection
([Sfikas et al., 2021](#bib.bib39); [Gallotta et al.,
2024](#bib.bib13)). Third, this work focused on the *outer loop*: which
item to evaluate next, and which pairs to retain. The inner hypothesis
generator was a single prompted LLM call, and could instead be a full
research agent ([Shang et al., 2025](#bib.bib40); [Lin et al.,
2026](#bib.bib26)); we kept it lightweight to show that the outer loop
is itself a meaningful lever, and expect the two to compose.

### A.2 Metrics over the run: all scenarios

Figure
[5](#A1.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ A.2 Metrics over the run: all scenarios ‣ Appendix A Additional results: maps and curves over the run for all scenarios ‣ QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via Quality–Diversity")
plots mean Quality, archive size $`n`$, and semantic Diversity against
the number of evaluations for all eight scenarios. Figure
[6](#A1.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ A.2 Metrics over the run: all scenarios ‣ Appendix A Additional results: maps and curves over the run for all scenarios ‣ QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via Quality–Diversity")
shows the same curves under the weaker proposer claude-haiku-4-5.

Unlike Quality, Diversity changes little after the first $`{\sim}100`$
evaluations, while archive size $`n`$ keeps growing. A likely reason is
that admission is decided by the LLM novelty check against nearest
neighbors, not by an embedding-distance threshold. New entries then add
distinct hypotheses within the region the archive already spans, which
raises $`n`$ but not the mean pairwise distance.

## Appendix B No-learning baselines: relevance-MMR and a quality-weighted DPP

To ask whether the online learning and archive machinery earns its cost,
we compare against two training-free re-rankers on Goodreads, where
Quality is a real human star rating that neither the learning methods
nor the baselines can game. *Relevance-MMR* ([Carbonell and Goldstein,
1998](#bib.bib6)) greedily selects items by
$`\gamma\cos(\text{item},\pi)-(1-\gamma)\max_{j\in S}\cos(\text{item},j)`$
over the same content embeddings, where $`S`$ is the set of items
selected so far. *Quality-weighted DPP* ([Chen et al., 2018](#bib.bib7))
is the principled counterpart: greedy MAP inference for a determinantal
point process maximizing
$`\gamma\sum_{i\in S}\mathrm{rel}_{i}+(1-\gamma)\log\det(L_{S})`$. Here
$`\mathrm{rel}_{i}=\cos(\text{item}_{i},\pi)`$ is the relevance of item
$`i`$, the same relevance MMR uses. The matrix $`L_{S}`$ holds the
pairwise cosine similarities of the items in $`S`$, so
$`\log\det(L_{S})`$ measures the diversity of the set as its log-volume.
In both baselines, the weight $`\gamma\in[0,1]`$ trades relevance
against diversity, and $`\gamma{=}1`$ recovers plain top-$`K`$ retrieval
exactly.

Neither baseline uses an archive, novelty filter, or feedback, and no
LLM touches anything that could affect the headline result: selection is
pure geometry over precomputed content embeddings, with relevance
$`\cos(\text{item},\pi)`$ rather than an LLM score (scoring the full
pool with an LLM is precisely the cost our setting excludes), and
Quality is the human star rating, fixed the moment an item is selected.
The only LLM calls are measurement plumbing: after selection, each
chosen item receives a zero-shot memo (proposer claude-sonnet-5) and the
same joint item+memo embedding the QD entries carry, so that Diversity
and Coverage are computed in the same embedding space as Table
[2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5.2 Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via Quality–Diversity")
and every row emits the same item–hypothesis artifact. These memos
cannot influence which items are selected or their ratings.

For each reader, the Coverage grid is fitted jointly to all QD, MMR, and
DPP rows using full SVD and the same 1% padding convention. This larger
reference pool differs from Table
[2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5.2 Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via Quality–Diversity"),
so absolute Coverage need not match across tables. The comparison is not
a controlled ablation of item selection, however: the QD variants
observe the rating of every item they evaluate (up to $`1{,}000`$ per
run) and use it for replacement and, in QD-Rec, for the bandit, whereas
the baselines see none. They are no-feedback geometric references, and
the gap measures what rating feedback and the archive machinery buy
together. Every run is matched in archive size $`n`$ to the QD-Rec
archive of its reader; selection is deterministic given the embeddings,
so rows are single runs (Table
[4](#A2.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Appendix B No-learning baselines: relevance-MMR and a quality-weighted DPP ‣ QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via Quality–Diversity")).

No setting of either baseline reaches any QD variant on Quality. The
baselines approach QD-Rec’s Diversity only at their most
diversity-favoring settings, and a few settings exceed its Coverage. The
DPP gives almost the same results as MMR, so the gap is not specific to
MMR’s heuristic.

## Appendix C Dataset details

This appendix gives the full dataset construction for the four domains
of Section
[5.1](#S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3 "Domains. ‣ 5.1 Setup ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via Quality–Diversity")
(sources, filtering, pool sizes, and the specific profiles used).

##### Goodreads (real human-feedback grounding).

We use the Children subset of the UCSD Goodreads Book Graph ([Wan and
McAuley, 2018](#bib.bib44)). For each reader, the candidate pool is
their own rated books (minus the few used to construct the profile), so
every item carries a ground-truth rating. We select two readers by a
fixed procedure, set before any experiment. A reader qualifies if they
meet six thresholds: at least $`200`$ rated books, at least $`500`$
written reviews, a rating standard deviation of at least $`0.9`$, at
least $`70\%`$ of shelved books marked as read, at least $`80\%`$ of
sampled reviews in English, and an entropy of at least $`2.0`$ nats in
their books’ distribution over shelves. Of the $`542{,}145`$ readers,
$`8`$ qualify. We take the qualifying reader with the most ratings, and
then the one with the most ratings whose most common shelf differs from
the first reader’s. This gives a picture-book reader ($`1{,}761`$ books)
and a series/young-adult reader ($`1{,}117`$ books). Goodreads uses the
reader’s $`1`$–$`5`$ rating in place of the LLM judge, so the bandit
reward is $`q(x)/5`$. In the local comparison, a new book replaces its
nearest neighbor only if its rating is strictly higher; ties keep the
incumbent. Books are selected without replacement in all three variants,
including seed books and discarded proposals, because a fixed rating
means a new memo for the same book would get the same score.

##### M&A target discovery.

We construct country-specific company universes from LSEG Workspace data
that combine (i) tabular financial snapshot features (as of 2024-08-31)
and (ii) textual business descriptions. We filter to a target country,
retain feature columns with at least 0.80 fill rate, and merge
description fields into a single company profile. This yields universes
of 6,332 USA companies. The profile $`\pi`$ is an acquirer selected from
the same universe; in our runs we use two USA acquirers, Walt Disney Co
and JPMorgan Chase & Co. For QD-Rec, each candidate company has a
precomputed embedding of its business description, used only for bandit
item selection. The proposer, the judge and the archive embedding use
the full company profile, which also includes the location, the industry
classification and the financial features.

##### Marketing.

We use a subset of the NVIDIA Nemotron-Personas-USA dataset, a
large-scale *synthetic customer-profile* corpus aligned to real-world US
demographic distributions ([Meyer and Corneil, 2025](#bib.bib31)). We
use this synthetic dataset as a proxy in lieu of sensitive real-world
customer data. Each customer profile includes demographic attributes
(e.g., age, sex, marital status, education, occupation, city/state) and
multiple profile facets (professional, sports, arts, travel, culinary).
To control for regional heterogeneity we restrict to a single state
(California) and sample 10,000 customer profiles for experiments. We use
two distinct product profiles (a desktop 3D printer and an online
upskilling subscription), spanning different purchase contexts (a
one-time tool purchase vs. career reskilling). The seed archive is
initialized from sampled customer profiles, and the three variants
iteratively generate and evaluate targeting hypotheses for additional
profiles.

##### Paper-abstract exploration.

We use a fixed collection of paper metadata (title and abstract only)
drawn from three recent machine-learning conferences: ICLR 2026, ICML
2026, and NeurIPS 2025. We filter to accepted statuses (Oral, Spotlight,
and Poster, plus ICLR’s conditional accepts) and retain entries with
non-empty identifier, title, and abstract, yielding 17,511 papers (5,358
/ 6,341 / 5,812 for ICLR / ICML / NeurIPS respectively). The metadata is
obtained from the papercopilot/paperlists repository ([Paper Copilot
(2026), Jing Yang](#bib.bib34)). We precompute candidate embeddings from
title+abstract for bandit item selection. Archive embeddings are
computed from the concatenated title, abstract, and memo
(item_hypothesis mode) and are used for novelty-neighbor retrieval,
semantic Diversity, and Coverage. The three variants generate memos for
selected papers and apply the same local novelty-first archive update
procedure.

## Appendix D Prompt Templates

This appendix lists the prompts used in our experiments. The three
variants use the same generation and judging prompts. They differ only
in how the next item is selected and whether the generator is shown
archive exemplars. For each domain we show the generator prompt, the
judge prompt (0–10 score), the novelty-check prompt, and the
pairwise-duel prompt, which runs only when an entry is not novel.
Goodreads has only the generator and novelty-check prompts, because it
uses human ratings for Quality and replacement. Placeholders such as
{acquirer_profile} are filled in at run time. A novelty-check or duel
response that cannot be parsed never adds an entry to the archive.

### D.1 Example Profiles Used in Experiments

Researcher profile used in ML Papers experiments: OpenEndedness
Researcher.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

An ML researcher working on open-ended and quality-diversity methods.
Their through-line is divergent search, reaching ambitious capabilities
through diverse intermediate stepping stones rather than direct climbs
toward a fixed objective, but in practice they bring a handful of
separable questions to a paper. Sometimes a paper is interesting for how
it measures novelty or behavioral diversity without hand-designed
descriptors, through learned representations and embeddings that define
what a good behavior space even is; sometimes for its archive and
selection mechanics, such as what to retain and how local competition
and illumination shape search; sometimes for its operators, such as
mutation, crossover, or using large models as variation operators;
sometimes for auto-curricula and co-evolution, where agents and the
environments that challenge them generate their own next problems;
sometimes for what it says about exploration and the deception of
objectives, including intrinsic motivation, when direct optimization
stalls, and what transfers from reinforcement-learning exploration; and
sometimes for recursive self-improvement, where systems rewrite their
own code, operators, or objectives so that gains compound, as in
self-referential and self-modifying agents. They have a skeptical streak
toward pure scaling and benchmark-chasing, and they actively look to
import techniques from adjacent areas into open-ended search. They do
not expect every paper at a major ML conference to be about
open-endedness; they look for the specific angle (a method, a
measurement, a failure mode, an assumption) that connects to their
interest.

Researcher profile used in ML Papers experiments: AI Startup Researcher.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

An applied ML researcher at an early-stage AI startup who reads research
through the lens of practical leverage. They are not only asking, "Could
this become a product?" but also, "Could this make a product cheaper,
safer, faster, more reliable, more defensible, easier to evaluate, or
easier to specialize?" Their interest is in papers that could plausibly
affect a 3-to-12-month startup roadmap, whether by enabling a new
product surface, improving unit economics, reducing inference cost,
increasing reliability, strengthening safety guarantees, opening a
vertical market, or creating a data or evaluation moat. When reading
papers from major ML conferences in particular, they do not expect every
paper to be immediately productizable. They recognize that much of this
work is theoretical, exploratory, or several steps removed from company
use, so they look for the subset of work that hints at future
engineering leverage, changes an important assumption, improves the
efficiency/safety/reliability envelope, or suggests a direction that
could compound into practical advantage over time.

Product profile used in Marketing experiments: 3D printer.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

LAYERCRAFT is a fictional desktop 3D-printer brand in the \$500-\$900
price range. It is aimed at people who already make, fix, or teach
things and want to do so with their own parts and designs, and it
positions itself as "the printer that just prints": the machine arrives
assembled and calibrated, and the first print starts within fifteen
minutes of unboxing.

The lineup comprises three models. "Layercraft Studio" is a compact,
fully enclosed printer, quiet enough for an apartment or a classroom.
"Layercraft Workshop" has a larger build volume and prints tougher
engineering materials for functional parts. "Layercraft Color" holds
four spools and switches between them automatically for multi-color
prints.

Every model has automatic bed leveling, a companion app with a library
of ready-to-print designs, and a 2-year warranty with US-based support.
A design marketplace lets owners sell or share their own models, and
educators get free lesson plans and a classroom management mode.
Filament is sold in recyclable spools at \$20-\$30 per kilogram.

Owners use it for different things: replacing a broken part on an
appliance or a car instead of ordering one; prototyping a product for a
small business or a side venture; STEM projects with children or
students; props, cosplay and tabletop-gaming pieces; custom organizers,
tools and gifts. It is not for everyone: it needs a permanent desk-sized
spot, a few evenings to learn basic 3D design and slicing, filament at
\$20-\$30 per kilogram, and patience, since a typical print takes
several hours.

LAYERCRAFT frames a 3D printer as a tool for people who make things,
like a sewing machine or a table saw: something that pays for itself in
the things it makes and the things it fixes. By taking the setup and the
failed prints out of the experience, it aims to make owning one ordinary
in that kind of household.

Product profile used in Marketing experiments: Upskilling.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

SkillForge is a fictional online learning platform offered at \$89-\$249
per month. Centered on business skills, technology, and creative fields,
it provides content aimed at practical, job-ready skill acquisition. Its
defining feature is that it is designed not as passive video-watching
but around the goal of "being able to use what you learn at work."

Courses are organized into three learning tracks. The "Business Track"
delivers skills that make you immediately useful in white-collar roles
-- data analysis, project management, financial modeling, presentation.
The "Tech Track" offers hands-on courses from the basics to applications
of Python, SQL, cloud, and AI, understandable even for non-engineers.
The "Creative Track" teaches expressive skills usable for side work and
career changes, such as UI/UX design, video editing, and writing.

Each course is taught by a working expert and includes a weekly live Q&A
session, a Slack community of fellow learners, and assignment
submissions with feedback modeled on real work. Progress is visualized
on a dashboard, and completion certificates can be posted on LinkedIn or
a portfolio. A corporate plan adds team-level enrollment management and
progress reporting.

The intended users are diverse: late-20s-to-30s professionals aiming to
upskill in their current jobs, women considering reskilling as they plan
a return from childcare, seniors preparing for a second career after
retirement, and employees with a side-gig mindset who want a source of
income beyond their main job.

With the concept of "making re-learning unremarkable," SkillForge is
designed so that even busy working adults can steadily build skills with
3-4 hours of study a week. With no enrollment fee and flexible,
cancel-anytime plans, it lowers the barrier to staying with learning and
aims to support the career autonomy of working people in the US.

Generate an acquisition hypothesis explaining why the acquirer should

Focus on:

- Financial attractiveness (valuation, growth trajectory, deal sizing

Be concrete and specific to the actual companies involved. Reference

this company; recommend against it only if the strategic fit is
genuinely poor.

Use the existing theses as inspiration. You may:

- \*\*Mutate\*\*: Take a strategic angle from ONE thesis and adapt it to
this new target

- \*\*Crossover\*\*: Combine elements from TWO OR MORE theses into a
novel rationale

- \*\*Explore\*\*: Propose a completely different strategic direction
not yet covered by any thesis

Also report which operator you used and the thesis number(s) you built
on, using the

"Thesis N" numbers shown above (leave the source list empty for
Explore).

Do not copy phrases verbatim from the existing theses.

Provide your response in this EXACT JSON format:

{

"operation": "mutate" \| "crossover" \| "explore",

"source_examples": \[thesis numbers you built on, e.g. \[2\] for mutate
or \[1, 3\] for crossover; \[\] for explore\],

"evolution_note": "ONE sentence on how the example thesis/theses shaped
this hypothesis, e.g. which angle came from which Thesis N. This is the
ONLY field that may reference the examples; leave empty for explore.",

value creation potential. Write it as a STANDALONE rationale, in the
same style as one written with no examples in front of you: do NOT

}

{hypothesis}

---

Score how compelling and plausible the strategic case for the
acquisition is, considering:

- Strategic fit with the acquirer’s existing business

- Synergy potential (revenue and cost synergies)

- Feasibility (is this acquisition realistic and executable?)

- Risk factors (integration challenges, market risks, regulatory
concerns)

- Value creation potential

A hypothesis that argues against the acquisition, concludes the target
is a poor fit, or offers only a hollow/implausible rationale is a weak

- 0-2: No real case (argues against, no strategic fit, or
hollow/implausible rationale)

- 3-4: Weak case (strained or generic rationale; major concerns)

- 5-6: Moderate case (some plausible merit but notable gaps)

- 7-8: Strong case (specific, plausible fit with clear value creation)

- 9-10: Excellent case (highly compelling, specific, plausible thesis)

"score": \<integer from 0-10\>

}

Scoring guide:

- 0-2: Poor recommendation (irrelevant/low-signal; likely a waste of
time)

- 3-4: Weak recommendation (thin connection; generic memo; few concrete
next steps)

- 5-6: OK / mixed (some relevance, but limited novelty or actionable
direction; unsurprising)

- 7: Good (clear relevance + shows specific, plausible research
directions)

- 8: Very good (strong relevance + multiple specific directions; minimal
hand-waving)

- 9-10: Exceptional (highly relevant, genuinely novel insight, very
interesting)

### D.5 Goodreads-Children (grounding)

Goodreads has no LLM quality judge (Quality is the reader’s held-out
star rating), so its prompt set is smaller: memo generation and the
novelty check. For a non-novel book, replacement compares its human
rating directly with that of its nearest neighbor: a strictly higher
rating replaces the neighbor, while a tie or lower rating retains the
incumbent. The bandit uses rating/5 for both seed initialization and
subsequent updates, while reported Quality remains on the 1–5 scale.
Previously tried books, including seeds, are excluded from subsequent
selection.

## Appendix E Example QD-Rec recommendations

Two QD-Rec recommendations from M&A and marketing (proposer
claude-sonnet-5, judge gpt-5.6-terra). Each was made by the mutate
operator from a single parent in the archive, and we chose them to show
how a parent hypothesis shapes the child. For each, we give the chosen
item, the parent hypothesis, the child hypothesis, and the hypothesis
that Novelty wrote for the same item without exemplars. Texts are
verbatim apart from the replacement of non-ASCII characters.

### M&A target discovery: JPMorgan Chase & Co (acquirer)

*Acquirer profile: JPMorgan Chase & Co. Hypothesis = acquisition thesis
(judge 0–10). QD-Rec run with seed 1; the child is evaluation 312 of
1,000, made by mutate from one parent. Scores: parent 1/10, child 5/10,
Novelty 1/10 (seed 2). The child entered the archive and was later
replaced by a nearby entry that won a pairwise duel against it.*

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

Company: Liberty TripAdvisor Holdings Inc

Location: Englewood, United States of America

Sector / Industry: Technology / Online Services

Activity: Online Services (NEC)

Enterprise Value (2024-08-31, local currency): 2083588988.12

YTD / 2Y total return (%): -49.4117647044217 / -35.7825567494573

Business Description:

Liberty TripAdvisor Holdings, Inc. operates as a family of brands that
connect people to experiences. The Company leverages its brands,
technology, and capabilities to connect its global audience with
partners through rich content, travel guidance, and two-sided
marketplaces for experiences, accommodations, restaurants, and other
travel categories. The Company operates through three segments: Brand
Tripadvisor, Viator, and TheFork. The Brand Tripadvisor segment includes
Tripadvisor-branded hotels, media and advertising, and Tripadvisor
experiences and dining business. The Viator segment provides an online
marketplace that allows travelers to research and book tours, activities
and attractions in travel destinations through its Viator branded
platform, which includes Website, mobile Web, and mobile app. TheFork
segment provides information and services for consumers to research and
book dining reservations through its dedicated online restaurant
reservations platform, TheFork.

Listing 35: Chosen item.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

Southwest Airlines is unusually well-suited to JPMorgan given the bank’s
existing role as issuer of the Southwest Rapid Rewards co-brand card
portfolio, one of the largest travel rewards programs in the country;
full ownership would let JPMorgan capture the entire loyalty-program
economics--breakage, points sales, and ancillary fee revenue--rather
than sharing them through an issuing partnership, mirroring how airline
loyalty programs elsewhere have been valued as standalone assets worth
more than the carrier itself. At an EV of \$15.3B, Southwest is trading
below its levels of two (\$15.8B) and four years ago (\$17.5B) despite a
modest 1.3% YTD gain, offering JPMorgan an opportunity to acquire a
top-tier domestic airline brand and its 100+ million-member loyalty base
at a valuation depressed by sector-wide fuel and margin pressure rather
than by any structural decline in Southwest’s franchise. Vertical
integration would let JPMorgan embed banking, financing, and payments
products directly into the travel purchase funnel--installment financing
for fares through Chase’s balance-sheet lending, bundled Chase Travel
booking, and richer transaction data for underwriting and cross-sell
into CCB’s card and deposit products. At roughly 1.6% of JPMorgan’s
~\$963B enterprise value, this is a financially digestible bolt-on that
diversifies earnings into a consumer-facing, high-frequency transaction
business while deepening an already-existing commercial relationship,
though it would require JPMorgan to underwrite genuine airline operating
risk (fuel, labor, capacity cycles) that sits outside its traditional
risk models.

Listing 36: Parent hypothesis, for Southwest Airlines Co (score 1/10).

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

Liberty TripAdvisor’s three marketplaces--Tripadvisor, Viator, and
TheFork--represent a global audience of travel researchers and bookers
that JPMorgan could plug directly into Chase Travel, its growing
proprietary booking platform, and into Chase Offers and Ultimate Rewards
redemption, capturing interchange, points-funded bookings, and
installment-financing revenue on activities, dining, and accommodations
that currently flow to third-party payment rails. At a \$2.08B
enterprise value--down sharply from \$3.39B three years ago and off 49%
YTD--the company is trading near a multi-year low, giving JPMorgan an
opportunity to acquire a recognizable global travel brand and its
two-sided marketplace infrastructure (Viator’s tours/activities network,
TheFork’s restaurant reservation footprint) at a depressed valuation
rather than paying peak multiples seen in prior years. Owning these
consumer touchpoints would also generate rich transaction and behavioral
data to sharpen underwriting and cross-sell into Chase’s card and
travel-rewards products, while TheFork’s European dining density and
Viator’s experiences marketplace diversify Chase’s travel ecosystem
beyond flights and hotels. At roughly 0.2% of JPMorgan’s ~\$963B
enterprise value, this is an immaterial-sized, easily digestible bolt-on
that extends the bank’s travel-commerce strategy into adjacent
categories at a cyclically discounted entry point.

Listing 37: QD-Rec child hypothesis (mutate, score 5/10).

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

This deal lacks strategic logic: JPMorgan is a diversified financial
holding company (banking, markets, asset management) while Liberty
TripAdvisor is a consumer travel marketplace business with no meaningful
overlap in capabilities, technology, or customer needs that JPMorgan
doesn’t already access via its Chase Travel platform and existing
card-linked travel partnerships. At roughly \$2.1B enterprise value
versus JPMorgan’s ~\$963B EV, the deal is immaterial in size and would
not move the needle financially, while Liberty TripAdvisor’s
deteriorating fundamentals (-49% YTD, -36% over two years, EV down from
~\$3.4B four years ago) signal a structurally challenged business facing
competitive pressure from Google, Booking Holdings, and Expedia in
online travel. JPMorgan’s core competitive advantages--balance sheet
scale, regulatory relationships, payments infrastructure, and wealth
management--do not translate into any obvious right-to-win in managing a
travel content and booking marketplace, and the segments (Viator,
TheFork, Tripadvisor media) would sit awkwardly within a bank holding
company’s risk and regulatory framework. Any travel-related synergy
JPMorgan seeks (e.g., enhancing Chase Sapphire travel benefits or Chase
Travel bookings) can be achieved more efficiently through commercial
partnerships or licensing rather than full acquisition and integration
of a publicly-troubled, sub-scale asset. We recommend against pursuing
this acquisition given the poor strategic fit and absence of compelling
synergy rationale.

Listing 38: Novelty hypothesis for the same item, written without
exemplars (score 1/10).

Novelty wrote its hypothesis for Liberty TripAdvisor without earlier
examples. It argued that JPMorgan’s existing Chase Travel platform and
commercial partnerships made an acquisition unnecessary, so it offered
no affirmative reason to buy the company (1/10). QD-Rec drew on an
archived hypothesis proposing that JPMorgan acquire Southwest Airlines.
The parent proposed integrating financing, payments and rewards into
travel purchases, and using transaction data to improve credit decisions
and offer related financial products. The judge recognized this
commercial rationale but scored the parent 1/10, citing restrictions on
bank ownership of an airline and exposure to fuel, labor and other
operating risks.

The mutate operator adapted this rationale to the travel marketplaces
described in Liberty TripAdvisor’s company information. The child
proposed connecting bookings for activities, dining and accommodation to
Chase Travel, rewards redemption and installment financing. It retained
the parent’s idea of linking travel purchases to financial services,
while changing the target from an airline to a travel platform. The
judge rated the child 5/10, although it still raised concerns about
competition, acquisition complexity and whether partnerships would
suffice. A parent rated only 1/10 thus served as a stepping stone for a
more highly rated recommendation about a different company.

In this example, the model generated statements and interpretations
absent from the input, including a loyalty base of more than 100 million
members. For example, [Southwest’s July 22, 2026
announcement](https://investors.southwest.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/1935/southwest-airlines-reports-second-quarter-2026-results-earnings-power-on-full-display)
came after the model’s knowledge cutoff and reported “nearly 100 million
Members.” We could not verify the claim of more than 100 million
members. The financial snapshot is dated August 2024, but note that
[Tripadvisor acquired Liberty TripAdvisor Holdings in April
2025](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1526520/000110465925041251/tm2513424d1_ex99-1.htm).
In this experiment, we supplied the model with only basic financial data
and short business descriptions. Using the recommendations for actual
decisions would require more detailed and up-to-date information.

Listing 39: Chosen item.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

Sharon’s explicit ambition to move from the classroom into a
district-wide leadership role--developing STEM curricula and mentoring
other teachers--requires competencies her ECE and STEM pedagogy training
doesn’t fully provide: project management to roll out a district-wide
program, data analysis to evaluate learning outcomes, and polished
presentation skills to advocate for inclusive policies to administrators
and school boards. SkillForge’s Business Track maps directly onto these
gaps, offering practical frameworks she could immediately apply while
still pursuing her master’s degree. Her comfort with structure,
spreadsheets, and hands-on STEM tools also makes the Tech Track’s
approachable Python and data courses appealing, letting her build
lightweight tools or dashboards to track her STEM curriculum’s
impact--something she could point to when pitching herself for a
curriculum specialist role. As someone who already devotes personal time
to maker-space workshops and mentoring at an after-school STEM club, the
platform’s weekly 3-4 hour commitment, live expert Q&As, and
LinkedIn-postable certificates fit naturally into her disciplined,
growth-oriented routine and would reinforce the professional credibility
she needs as she transitions from teaching into educational leadership.

Listing 40: Parent hypothesis, for Sharon English, 46, preschool or
kindergarten teacher (score 7/10).

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

Jesus’s stated goal of becoming a charge nurse and eventually launching
a preventive health outreach program in National City requires
competencies his clinical training never covered--project management to
coordinate a screening initiative, basic data analysis to track and
report health outcomes, and polished presentation skills to pitch the
program to hospital administrators or grant funders. SkillForge’s
Business Track speaks directly to that gap, while the Tech Track’s
approachable data courses could let him build simple dashboards to
demonstrate the impact of his community screenings, reinforcing his
evidence-based, protocol-driven mindset. His per-shift, flexible work
schedule and self-described tendency toward disorganization make the
platform’s structured 3-4 hour weekly cadence, dashboard progress
tracking, and cancel-anytime plan especially appealing, since it offers
accountability without locking him into a rigid semester-style
commitment. A LinkedIn-postable certificate would also lend credibility
as he positions himself for charge-nurse responsibilities and eventually
a leadership role serving underserved Latino patients. While SkillForge
can’t replace the BSN or FNP coursework he ultimately needs, it fills a
real and immediate void in the program-management and advocacy skills
his broader career vision demands, making him a solid niche fit despite
the platform’s non-clinical focus.

Listing 41: QD-Rec child hypothesis (mutate, score 7/10).

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

Jesus’s near-term career goals are almost entirely clinical--finishing
his BSN, becoming an FNP, and building a community health outreach
program--none of which SkillForge’s business, tech, or creative tracks
can substitute for, since it offers no accredited nursing or healthcare
credentialing. While he might be mildly drawn to the Business Track’s
project management or data analysis modules to sharpen his charge-nurse
leadership and eventually structure a preventive-screening program, this
is a peripheral use case rather than a core need, and his already packed
per-shift schedule plus stated preference for unstructured downtime
(hiking, guitar, cooking) makes committing another 3-4 hours weekly to a
subscription-based platform a hard sell. Because the platform’s value
proposition of ’job-ready skills for white-collar/tech/creative careers’
doesn’t map onto his actual professional trajectory, and he shows no
expressed interest in side-gig income streams like UI/UX or video
editing, SkillForge is a poor strategic fit for this persona despite
superficial overlap in the ’practical skill-building’ ethos.

Listing 42: Novelty hypothesis for the same item, written without
exemplars (score 2/10).

Novelty focused on the nurse’s clinical career goals and SkillForge’s
lack of accredited nursing courses. It recognized that project
management and data analysis could help with his planned screening
program, but treated these as peripheral needs and his shift work as an
obstacle to study. It concluded that the platform was a poor fit (2/10).
QD-Rec drew on an archived hypothesis about a preschool teacher seeking
district-wide curriculum leadership. The parent argued that SkillForge
could supply project management, data analysis and presentation skills
needed for this transition but not fully covered by her teaching
training (7/10).

The mutate operator applied this reasoning to the nurse’s ambition to
lead a team and launch a community screening program. The child
connected project management to coordinating screenings, data analysis
to reporting health outcomes, and presentation skills to securing
support from hospital administrators or funders. These skills became the
main reason to recommend SkillForge as a complement to his clinical
education. The child also argued that the platform’s flexible format
could suit his irregular schedule. The judge found the connection
between his leadership goals and the courses credible and rated the
child 7/10. Reusing the teacher’s hypothesis helped QD-Rec connect the
nurse’s leadership goals to courses that Novelty had dismissed as
peripheral.
````
